It sounds a lot like it may be a bug upstream. A quick look at issues on the .NET repositories showed me a few things you could try.

Some users reported hangs caused by permission issues. Like you said, I would also expect a privilege error in this case, but maybe the logic in the dotnet CLI that handles this has a bug. You could try a [manual install](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/install/linux-scripted-manual#manual-install) or a [scripted install](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/install/linux-scripted-manual#scripted-install) on a user-accessible directory.

> [!NOTE]
> As per the documentation, this kind of install is not recommended for setting up a development environment and it's only meant for CI scenarios. The recommendation for Linux users is to install the .NET SDK using their distro's package manager (or, if not available, the Microsoft package repository). However, this will allow us to test if it's a permission issue.

Both the manual install and the scripted install are downloading the .NET SDK in a `.tar.gz` compressed archive. The only difference is the script will auto-detect what to download based on your system and extract it (by default in `$HOME/.dotnet`), whereas in the manual install you have to select the right one. In both cases, you still need to set the environment variables `DOTNET_ROOT` and `PATH`.

Before executing the dotnet CLI command, make sure to set the environment variable `DOTNET_ROOT` to the directory where you extracted the .NET SDK (should be `$HOME/.dotnet` if you used the default install directory with the scripted install).

Then, add the `DOTNET_ROOT` directory to the environment variable `PATH` before any other directory that contains the dotnet CLI binary so it takes precedence, or use the full path when running the dotnet CLI command.

Here's an example script that does everything and then runs the dotnet CLI command to build the Godot project (according to the path in the MRP):

```bash
#!/bin/bash

# Use dotnet-install script to install the latest .NET SDK.
curl -L https://dot.net/v1/dotnet-install.sh -o dotnet-install.sh
chmod +x ./dotnet-install.sh
./dotnet-install.sh --version latest

# Set environment variables.
export DOTNET_ROOT=$HOME/.dotnet
export PATH=$DOTNET_ROOT:$PATH

# Build the Godot project.
dotnet build /home/foreverexe/godottest/GodotTest.csproj -c Debug -v detailed
```

Modify the script if needed. Feel free to delete the `$HOME/.dotnet` directory afterwards. You can also specify a different install directory with `--install-dir` (see [`dotnet-install`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/tools/dotnet-install-script) documentation).

If that doesn't work, it may not be a permission issue. You can also try disabling other parts of the build logic that may be causing the hang:

- Set the environment variable `DOTNET_CLI_DISABLE_PROJECT_EVAL` to `true` before running the dotnet CLI command. If that works, then the hang is in the project evaluation logic.
- Set the flag `--no-restore` in the dotnet CLI command. If that works, then the hang is likely in the NuGet restore logic.
- Some users also reported getting hangs with MSBuild node reuse, so you could try setting the environment variable `MSBUILDDISABLENODEREUSE` to `1` and see if that helps.

Let me know if any of this helped.

Packages are downloaded from the available NuGet source feeds unless they are already available in your NuGet packages directory. By default, the only source feed available will be nuget.org, and the packages directory is `$HOME/.nuget/packages` in Linux.

Judging from your error message, it looks like you may not be able to access nuget.org so it can't retrieve the packages.

> It seems that it cannot find the NuGet package, if I'm correct. For me, it's always on the Desktop since for comfort I extract the Godot executable + the GodotSharp folder and place it there to access the editor immediately.

The `GodotSharp` directory included in the compressed archive needs to be next to the Godot editor executable because it will load some of those DLLs directly for editor integration.

However, the `Godot.NET.Sdk`, `GodotSharp`, and `GodotSharpEditor` packages used by the C# project are different. These are retrieved using the normal .NET restore process which doesn't know anything about the `GodotSharp` directory, instead it will use your configured NuGet source feeds (by default nuget.org) to retrieve them. You could technically create a custom source feed and add the packages there or install them to your packages directory, but I wouldn't recommend it.

It looks like your computer is unable to access nuget.org. Are you perhaps behind a proxy or VPN that could be causing issues?

I don't think there is an issue with your NuGet configuration, but it should be fine to remove the `$HOME/.nuget/NuGet/NuGet.config` file, it will be recreated by NuGet on the next restore. You may want to back it up if you have custom configuration that you may want to keep. For reference, this is how the default looks like:

```xml
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8"?>
<configuration>
  <packageSources>
    <add key="nuget.org" value="https://api.nuget.org/v3/index.json" protocolVersion="3" />
  </packageSources>
</configuration>
```

You may also add custom NuGet configuration that only affects a specific C# project by creating a `NuGet.config` file next to the `.csproj` file.

But it sounds more like a network issue to me. There are a number of issues in the https://github.com/NuGet/Home repo that sound similar to what you are describing.

From reading some of those issues, it looks like trying to add a package may offer more information. For example: `dotnet add package Newtonsoft.Json`. Some users were getting an error on formating the Linux system information, but it appears that bug was fixed a while ago.

> feels like it would be better to make a local source pointing to the `GodotSharp` folder, since I imagine the engine uses these ones instead of something online.

The engine fetches dependencies from nuget.org, and we'll likely stop distributing the packages with the Editor download since it increases the download size for no reason. You are free to manually download the packages from nuget.org, but it's going to be a more convoluted process which is why I don't recommend it.

But if it works fine for you, feel free to create a [custom NuGet source feed](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/contributing/development/compiling/compiling_with_dotnet.html#nuget-packages) like we do for engine development, or manually add the packages to your NuGet packages directory (`$HOME/.nuget/packages`). Either of these options should work, but it requires more manual effort from you that you'll have to repeat for each new version of Godot that you download (and for every other NuGet package you may want to add to your projects).

Since this looks like a NuGet bug, unrelated to Godot, I would strongly suggest to look at existing issues in the [NuGet/Home](https://github.com/NuGet/Home) repo or reporting a new issue if an existing issue does not exist. Sorry I couldn't be of more help.

I'm back with good news, after a quick trip in the NuGet realms, and then a bit into dotnet's, **the issue was regarding IPV6 connectivity**. 
Apparently, on Nobara / Fedora `dotnet` was trying to connect using IPV6 but it clashes in some way, preventing in/outbound connections.

It now compiles without a single problem, now I have to look for a way to disable the IPV6 connection inside Godot instead of  prepending `DOTNET_SYSTEM_NET_DISABLEIPV6=1` every time outside of the editor. I would prefer to avoid disabling IPV6 system-wide.


# For the people that will stumble upon this issue and could be in the same situation
Try using `DOTNET_SYSTEM_NET_DISABLEIPV6=1 dotnet build your/project -c debug -v detailed`, it could be just a IPV6 incompatibility.
